short: a thing with its own identity that you look up or count, like a customer or an order. it becomes a table with a key.
how many rows on one side of a relationship can go with one row on the other: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many.
a table with a foreign key to each side of a many-to-many relationship, one row per pair, holding the relationship's own columns.
a minimal set of columns that identifies a row: drop any column and it stops being unique. a table can have several.
a key that comes from the world, like an email, an isbn or a sku. readable, and it can change.
a key the database makes up, like an identity number or a uuid. it never changes, and it doesn't stop duplicate entities on its own.
a key made of more than one column, like (order_id, line_no). its column order is the order of its index.
a boolean expression every row must not make false. NULL passes, because unknown isn't false.
a UNIQUE option (postgres 15) that treats NULLs as equal, so a second NULL is a duplicate.
a constraint whose check can wait until the end of the statement or, if deferred, until COMMIT.
adds a constraint without checking existing rows; new rows are checked at once, and VALIDATE CONSTRAINT checks the old ones later without blocking writes.
a CHECK or foreign key (postgres 18) that's recorded in the catalog but never checked.
what a foreign key does when its parent row is deleted or re-keyed: NO ACTION, RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL or SET DEFAULT.
X → Y: any two rows that agree on X agree on Y. a rule from what the columns mean; data can only disprove it.
everything a set of columns determines, found by applying dependencies until nothing new is added. all columns means a superkey.
the same fact stored in several rows, so an update to one copy leaves the others disagreeing. its siblings are the insert and delete anomalies.
Boyce-Codd normal form: every determinant of a non-trivial dependency is a key. 3NF almost always is BCNF.
a split of one table into several whose join gives back exactly the original rows. splitting along a dependency guarantees it.
storing a derivable fact twice on purpose, like a count or a total, to make reads cheaper. something has to keep the copy right.
a single row many transactions update, like a global counter. each update waits for the previous one's row lock.
a tree stored as one parent pointer per row, like manager_id. walked with a recursive CTE.
a tree stored as one row per (ancestor, descendant) pair, so subtree and ancestor queries are one lookup.
a tree stored as each row's path from the root, like 1.2.5, so a subtree is a prefix match. ltree is postgres's type for it.
a tree numbered by a depth-first walk, each node holding lft and rgt; a subtree is a range, and an insert renumbers.
marking a row as gone, usually with deleted_at, instead of deleting it. every query and constraint still sees the row.
a log of changes, one row per insert, update or delete, usually written by a trigger in the same transaction.
a generalised UNIQUE: no two rows may satisfy an operator, like && for overlapping ranges. enforced by a GiST index.
a key unique per moment: the same key may repeat as long as its ranges don't overlap. WITHOUT OVERLAPS in postgres 18.
entity-attribute-value: one row per cell, every value text. no types, no constraints, a join per attribute.
a reference made of a type string and an id, pointing into a different table per row. no foreign key can check it.
a named query that stores no rows. the rewriter pastes it into every query that uses it.
makes an updatable view refuse inserts and updates whose result it wouldn't show.
a view option (postgres 15) that checks the caller's rights on the underlying tables instead of the view owner's.
a query's result stored as a table, stale until REFRESH. CONCURRENTLY keeps readers going and needs a unique index.
the list of schemas postgres searches for an unqualified name. a better-typed function anywhere on it can hijack a call.
a user, a group, or both. it gets rights on objects with GRANT and nothing by default.
policies that add a condition to every query on a table: USING for rows you see, WITH CHECK for rows you write.
